title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD FOR A SIGN… BUT WHAT IF HE’S ALREADY GIVEN YOU A COMMAND YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD FOR A SIGN… BUT WHAT IF HE’S ALREADY GIVEN YOU A COMMAND YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING?

What if the silence you're calling God's absence is actually the space between what He has already told you and what you're still unwilling to surrender? This may be the hardest answer to prayer you've ever had to face.
There is a prayer that sounds holy.
It sounds humble. It sounds patient. It even sounds like faith.
“Lord, just give me a sign.”
You've whispered it with tears in your eyes.
You've prayed it before making decisions. Before leaving relationships. Before forgiving someone who shattered your trust. Before walking away from something you knew was slowly destroying your soul.
“God, if this is really You, show me.”
And sometimes, asking God for guidance is exactly what we should do.
But there is another possibility.
One we rarely want to consider.
What if you aren't waiting because God hasn't spoken?
What if you're waiting because you don't like what He already said?
Read that again.
Because somewhere between your unanswered prayers and your unfinished obedience, there may be a truth you've been trying desperately not to confront.
Not every season of waiting is rebellion.
Not every unanswered question means you've ignored God.
But sometimes the greatest obstacle to our spiritual growth isn't that we cannot hear God's voice.
It's that we already understand His Word—and we're hoping He will eventually tell us something different.
And the frightening part?
We can become so comfortable asking for another sign that we forget the command we've already received.
There was a man in Scripture who came to Jesus with a question that sounded sincere.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted to know what he needed to do.
He had kept commandments. He had lived a respectable life. From the outside, he appeared to be exactly the kind of person religious people would admire.
But Jesus saw what nobody else could see.
Mark 10:21 tells us:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.”
Don't rush past those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus confronted him, He loved him.
Before Jesus exposed what was holding his heart captive, He loved him.
And then Jesus told him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The man's response was devastating.
He went away sorrowful.
Why?
Because he had great possessions.
He had come asking Jesus about life, but when Jesus called him to surrender what ruled his heart, he walked away.
The tragedy wasn't that Jesus had refused to answer him.
The tragedy was that Jesus had answered him—and the answer revealed what he loved more.
Notice something else.
Jesus didn't chase him down and offer an easier version of discipleship.
He didn't say, “Never mind. Keep everything. Just follow Me when you're comfortable.”
The call remained.
And the man walked away grieving.
Perhaps that is where this story begins to feel uncomfortably familiar.
Because we, too, can approach Jesus asking for direction while quietly protecting the very thing His Word is confronting.
We ask God to restore our peace while refusing to release bitterness.
We ask Him to bless a relationship while ignoring what Scripture teaches about holiness and faithfulness.
We ask Him to change our hearts while continuing to feed the habits that harden them.
We ask Him to show us our purpose while overlooking the ordinary opportunities to love, serve, forgive, and speak truth already in front of us.
And sometimes we ask Him to open a door because we cannot bear the thought of closing one ourselves.
But here is what makes the Gospel so beautiful.
The Jesus who confronts you is the same Jesus who loves you.
His commands are not a cruel attempt to deprive you of life.
They are the words of the Savior who knows where life is found.
In John 14:15, Jesus says:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
The Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
A faithful rendering is:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
The verb τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from τηρέω (tēreō), meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
Jesus is not describing a transaction where we purchase His love through flawless performance.
He is describing the relationship between genuine love and obedience.
Obedience does not earn salvation.
It is a fitting response to the Savior who saves by grace.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because if you believe God will only love you after you obey perfectly, you'll spend your life terrified of failure.
But if you understand that Christ loved sinners enough to die for them, you'll begin to see obedience not merely as an obligation—but as a response of love.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
Not the other way around.
But somewhere along the way, many of us have confused seeking God's guidance with negotiating His authority.
We say, “Lord, lead me.”
But quietly add, “As long as You lead me somewhere I already want to go.”
We say, “Lord, use me.”
But add, “Just don't ask me to give up what makes me comfortable.”
We say, “Lord, change me.”
But hope He will leave our favorite sins untouched.
And then we wonder why our spiritual lives feel divided.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Luke that should make every person who claims to follow Jesus examine their heart.
Jesus asks in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
Imagine hearing that question directly from Christ.
Not from an angry preacher.
Not from someone trying to shame you.
From Jesus.
The One who healed the sick.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who wept at a tomb.
The One who would stretch out His arms on a Roman cross for people who could never save themselves.
“Why do you call Me Lord, but refuse to do what I say?”
What would you answer?
Would you tell Him you were waiting for confirmation?
Would you tell Him you needed more time?
Would you tell Him you were afraid?
Or would you finally tell Him the truth?
“Lord, I know what Your Word says. I'm just struggling to surrender.”
And perhaps that is the most honest prayer you've prayed in years.
Because spiritual maturity doesn't begin when we become experts at sounding faithful.
It grows when we stop pretending before the God who already knows us completely.
There is another scene in Scripture.
A wedding.
A celebration.
And suddenly, a problem.
The wine has run out.
Mary brings the need to Jesus.
Then she turns to the servants and speaks words that have echoed through centuries.
John 2:5:
“Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.”
Simple.
Uncomfortable.
Powerful.
Whatever He tells you, do it.
Not whatever feels convenient.
Not whatever everyone else approves.
Not whatever guarantees you won't be misunderstood.
Whatever He tells you.
Jesus instructs the servants to fill the waterpots with water.
And they do.
They fill them to the brim.
The water becomes wine through the power of Christ.
The servants did not manufacture the miracle through obedience.
Jesus performed the miracle.
But they obeyed the instruction they had received.
And that distinction matters.
Your obedience cannot create God's power. But your disobedience should never be disguised as waiting for His guidance.
You cannot force a miracle by doing enough religious things.
You cannot guarantee that God will give you the outcome you want by following a formula.
The Lord is sovereign.
His wisdom is greater than ours.
But when His Word is clear, the faithful response is not to demand an extraordinary sign before doing what He has already commanded.
It is to trust Him.
Even when obedience costs something.
Especially then.
Maybe you've been waiting for God to give you a sign that it's time to forgive.
But Ephesians 4:32 already calls believers to forgive one another as God in Christ has forgiven them.
That doesn't mean pretending the harm never happened.
It doesn't mean returning to an abusive relationship or removing necessary boundaries.
It means refusing to make vengeance the master of your heart.
Maybe you've been asking God whether you should confess the truth.
But 1 John 1:9 already assures us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Maybe you're asking if you should stop hiding a destructive pattern.
But Proverbs 28:13 warns against concealing sin and points toward mercy for those who confess and forsake it.
Maybe you've been waiting for permission to love someone who cannot repay you.
But Jesus has already called His followers to love even their enemies.
Maybe you're asking God whether your life matters.
But Scripture already declares that human beings are made in God's image, and the Gospel announces that Christ came to seek and save the lost.
And maybe the thing you most need to hear today is not a new revelation.
Maybe it is the Word you've been avoiding because you know it will change how you live.
But be careful here.
Because there is a danger in turning this message into another weapon against wounded people.
Some of you are not resisting a clear command.
You are exhausted.
You are grieving.
You are trying to make a difficult decision where Scripture gives principles but does not name the exact choice.
You are wondering which job to accept, whether to move, how to care for someone you love, or what the next season of life should look like.
And you desperately want wisdom.
There is no shame in that.
James 1:5 invites those who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
Seeking wise counsel, praying patiently, examining Scripture, and waiting for clarity can all be acts of faith.
God has not promised that every major life decision will arrive with a supernatural sign.
Nor should every coincidence, emotion, dream, or open door be treated as a divine command.
We must test what we believe against Scripture.
We must seek wisdom.
We must refuse to use supposed private revelations to contradict God's revealed truth.
And we must remember that waiting on God can be faithful obedience too.
The question is not whether you have ever asked for a sign.
The question is whether you're using the desire for a sign to avoid something God has already made clear.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that brings this into sharper focus.
שְׁמַע — Shema.
It appears at the beginning of Deuteronomy 6:4:
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.”
The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע (shama) means to hear or listen and, depending on context, can carry the sense of heeding or obeying.
That connection matters.
Biblical listening is not always merely receiving information.
It often calls for a response.
A person can hear the words of God without allowing those words to govern their life.
James later makes the same distinction with startling clarity.
James 1:22 says:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”
Deceiving yourselves.
Not merely misunderstanding.
Not merely forgetting.
Deceiving.
That is what makes this so serious.
We can accumulate sermons, devotionals, Bible studies, Christian videos, and inspirational quotes while remaining unwilling to obey the very truths we keep consuming.
We can know the language of surrender without surrendering.
We can know the vocabulary of repentance without turning from sin.
We can post about trusting God while secretly insisting on controlling every outcome.
And we can become skilled at recognizing truth without letting truth confront us.
But the purpose of Scripture is not to make us impressive religious spectators.
It is to lead us to Christ and equip us for a life shaped by His truth.
And that brings us to a man who once stood on the wrong side of God's will while believing he was defending it.
Saul.
A man zealous for religion.
A man convinced he was right.
A man persecuting followers of Jesus.
Then, on the road to Damascus, everything changed.
The risen Christ confronted him.
Saul's certainty collapsed.
The man who had been moving with violent confidence suddenly found himself blind and dependent on others.
Acts 9 records the encounter.
And what followed was not merely a change of opinion.
It was the beginning of a transformed life.
The persecutor became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The man who had tried to destroy the church became a servant of the Gospel.
But notice what made his story extraordinary.
It wasn't simply that Saul received a dramatic encounter.
It was that the risen Jesus Christ changed the direction of his life.
And that is the difference between chasing spiritual experiences and following the Savior.
A powerful moment may get your attention.
But discipleship involves trusting Christ with the life that follows.
Saul, later known as Paul, would eventually write about being crucified with Christ and living by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave Himself for him.
Not merely impressed by Jesus.
Not merely interested in Jesus.
Belonging to Jesus.
And maybe that's where this message is becoming personal.
Because you don't need another emotional experience if what you are avoiding is the ordinary, costly obedience of following Christ.
You may need to apologize.
You may need to tell the truth.
You may need to stop excusing a sin you've repeatedly renamed as a weakness.
You may need to seek help for something you cannot overcome alone.
You may need to make restitution where possible.
You may need to reconcile where reconciliation is safe and appropriate.
You may need to stop measuring God's faithfulness by whether He gives you the answer you prefer.
Or maybe you need to return to the simple things you've neglected.
Prayer.
Scripture.
Fellowship.
Service.
Love.
Faithfulness when nobody is watching.
Because not every act of obedience is dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like putting down the phone and finally praying honestly.
Sometimes it looks like telling your spouse the truth.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to join in cruelty when everyone else is laughing.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible after months of spiritual distance.
Sometimes it looks like reaching out to a trusted pastor or mature believer and admitting, “I need help.”
Sometimes it looks like saying, “Jesus, I cannot change myself. Please teach me to follow You.”
And sometimes the bravest spiritual decision of your life happens in a room where nobody applauds.
No audience.
No dramatic music.
No visible miracle.
Just a trembling heart choosing to obey the Lord.
But there is something even deeper you must understand.
God is not asking you to save yourself through obedience.
If that were possible, there would have been no need for the cross.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to give humanity a better list of instructions.
He came to redeem sinners.
To bear sin.
To reconcile us to God.
To accomplish what our righteousness could never accomplish.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we finally obeyed everything.
Not after we cleaned up every scandal.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy of grace.
While we were sinners.
He died for us.
And He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you can climb your way into God's acceptance by performing enough good deeds.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Savior, died for our sins and was raised from the dead, and that forgiveness and new life are found in Him.
Repentance is not a payment for mercy.
Faith is not a spiritual performance.
We come to Christ empty-handed.
And the grace that receives us also begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 describes the grace of God as teaching us to turn away from ungodliness and live godly lives.
Think about that.
Grace doesn't merely forgive your past.
Grace trains you for a different future.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without struggle.
Not without tears.
But genuinely.
And this is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because some of you know what it means to have a past you wish you could erase.
You know the shame of making promises to God and breaking them.
You know what it feels like to return to a habit you swore you would abandon.
You know the humiliation of realizing that the person you presented to the world was not the person you were becoming in secret.
You know what it's like to stand in church and sing about surrender while silently holding on to something that is destroying you.
And perhaps you have wondered whether God is tired of hearing your voice.
Whether you've exhausted His patience.
Whether your failures have finally made you unreachable.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to minimize your sin.
The answer is to look at your Savior.
Remember Peter.
The disciple who declared his loyalty.
The disciple who promised he would never abandon Jesus.
The disciple who denied Him three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of the warning.
The terrible realization of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
His confidence had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
His denial was real.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's restoration did not mean his denial was harmless.
It meant the grace of Christ was greater than Peter's failure.
The same man who once denied knowing Jesus would later boldly proclaim Him.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because Jesus is mighty to save.
Not because obedience is optional.
But because forgiveness restores us to a life of following Him.
Not because our past disappears from history.
But because our past does not have to remain the master of our future.
And perhaps, today, the command you've been avoiding is the simplest and most important one of all.
Repent.
Turn to Christ.
Stop running.
Stop hiding behind religious language.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to come home.
Jesus proclaimed in Mark 1:15:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
In Greek, the words include:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
The word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) calls for repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin toward God.
The word πιστεύετε (pisteuete) calls for faith, for believing the good news.
Both are present-tense imperatives in this passage, expressing the call to repent and believe.
This is not merely an invitation to feel bad about your mistakes.
It is a summons to turn toward the Savior.
And it is not merely an invitation to agree that Jesus exists.
It is a call to trust Him.
The Lord who commands repentance is the Lord who offers forgiveness.
The Lord who calls us to follow Him is the Lord who gave His life for sinners.
And the Lord who exposes what is hidden is the Lord who can cleanse what we cannot repair.
So perhaps the prayer that needs to change today is not, “God, give me another sign.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me where I have been resisting Your Word.”
“Give me wisdom where I genuinely do not know what to do.”
“Give me courage where I already know what is right.”
“Forgive me for confusing delay with discernment.”
“Teach me to obey You out of love, not fear.”
“Help me trust Your goodness even when following You costs me something.”
And above all:
“Jesus, I belong to You. Lead me.”
You may not receive the extraordinary confirmation you've been hoping for.
You may not see every outcome in advance.
You may not understand why obedience must be difficult.
But you have something greater than a passing sign.
You have the testimony of Scripture.
You have the promises of God.
You have the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And for those who belong to Him, you have the Holy Spirit, who leads believers in truth and produces fruit in lives surrendered to Christ.
Don't mistake the absence of a spectacular experience for the absence of God's guidance.
And don't mistake a difficult command for a lack of His love.
The cross has already settled how far Christ was willing to go to rescue sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
What is the one thing you already know God's Word is calling you to do, but you've been postponing?
Not the thing someone is pressuring you to do.
Not the thing fear is screaming at you to do.
Not a private impression that contradicts Scripture.
The thing you can honestly recognize as consistent with the teachings of Jesus.
What would obedience look like today?
Not next year.
Not when every circumstance becomes convenient.
Today.
Maybe you cannot fix everything immediately.
Maybe you need counsel, support, and time.
Maybe the first step is small.
But a small step of genuine faith is not insignificant.
And if you've fallen, don't make despair your permanent home.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Receive His mercy.
Rise and follow Him again.
The Gospel is not a story about flawless people who never stumble.
It is the good news of a perfect Savior who rescues sinners and teaches them to walk in newness of life.
“Lord, give me courage to obey.”

And if Jesus has already brought you through a season when surrender felt impossible, share a little of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may be one step away from giving up, and your words may encourage them to turn back to Christ.
Don't underestimate the power of a truthful testimony.
There are people who will never enter a church this week but may read a Gospel message on their phone tonight.
Someone may be carrying shame that only the grace of Jesus can answer.
Someone may be searching for a reason to believe that restoration is still possible.
Not because following a page saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because daily Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, and honest conversations about repentance, forgiveness, healing, and discipleship can help keep our attention on the One who does.
These resources are meant to help believers return to Scripture, understand the Gospel, and grow in faithful discipleship.
And there is another way you can become part of this mission.

Scripture encourages generosity in supporting Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
That is why I want to be clear about something important.
You do not have to pay for God's love, blessing, forgiveness, or approval.
It can help make this mission sustainable.
It can help us continue reaching people who may never have heard the Gospel explained with clarity, compassion, and conviction.
And it can help keep free discipleship resources available to those who cannot afford to pay.
It is a voluntary partnership in the work.
These products are simply expressions of the ministry and reminders of biblical truth. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is the reason.
You are still welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Keep growing in the Word.
The mission is not to build a community where people feel they must pay to belong.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ—the Savior whose grace cannot be bought.
Because the greatest gift you could ever receive was already purchased at a cost none of us could afford.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
But through the precious blood of Christ.
And now, before you leave this message, return to that question you came here carrying.
“God, will You give me a sign?”
Perhaps He will guide you through circumstances.
Perhaps He will give you wisdom through Scripture, prayer, and godly counsel.
Perhaps the answer will require patient waiting.
But if He has already spoken clearly through His Word, don't demand another sign as a condition of obedience.
Remember the rich young ruler.
Remember the servants at Cana.
Remember Saul on the Damascus road.
Remember Peter after his denial.
And most of all, remember Jesus.
The One who loved the rich young ruler even as He confronted his misplaced treasure.
The One whose power transformed water into wine.
The risen Lord who turned a persecutor into a witness.
The Savior who restored a disciple broken by his own denial.
The crucified and risen King who still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him.
The question is no longer merely whether you will receive another sign.
The question is whether you will trust the Savior who has already spoken.
And if you've been running, today can be the day you turn around.
Not because you finally became worthy.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
Not because you can rewrite your own history.
But because His grace can redeem what sin has broken and transform the life you place in His hands.
One day, you may realize that the answer you kept begging heaven to send was already waiting in the words of Jesus you were afraid to obey.
